supplement.holds: Contents and supplement-only statistics are not specified in the saved PDF. The article links supplementary material and says original contributions are included in the article/Supplementary material (p. 14, Data availability statement and Supplementary material). The 15-page PDF ends with references and has no appended supplement or embedded files. Main-text creative-performance statistics are available in Table 1 (p. 8), Table 2 (p. 9), and section 4.1 (p. 11). During finalization on 2026-10-09, Python urllib requests using User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 to the stated Frontiers URL and then https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1508383 both failed with WinError 10013 (socket access forbidden), as they had during reconciliation. Supplementary contents remain unverified.

paper_design_summary: In a controlled university design laboratory in Eastern China, 64 undergraduate design students were assigned to AIGC-assisted design or traditional design tools; section 3.1 explicitly states random assignment despite the quasi-experimental label in section 3.2.1 (p. 4). They completed an intelligent walking-cane design task using either chatbot dialogue and image generation or internet research and conventional design software, and design experts scored the submitted works using the Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale (pp. 5-6, sections 3.2.3, 3.3.1 and 3.4). EEG recordings and interviews assessed physiological states and experiences, without adding creative-output outcomes.

studies.label: Intelligent walking cane design: AIGC versus traditional design tools

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were assigned to the AIGC experimental group or the traditional-software control group. Cluster random sampling describes recruitment; the subsequent assignment statement refers to participants. The experiment took place in a controlled multimedia classroom at the Design Innovation Laboratory, with conditions in separate rooms. The explicit random-assignment statement supports lab_rct despite the conflicting quasi-experimental label.
assignment.quote: They were randomly assigned to either the experimental group (n = 32; 17 females, 15 males) or the control group (n = 32; 16 females, 16 males).
assignment.locator: p. 4, section 3.1 Participants (random assignment and recruitment); p. 4, section 3.2.1 Research variables (quasi-experimental label); p. 4, section 3.2.2 Equipment (controlled laboratory); p. 5, section 3.2.3 Research procedure (separate rooms).
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is reported in the supplied article; methods are on pp. 4-7.

arms.name: Experimental group (AIGC)
arms.description: ChatGPT, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion were provided as AIGC tools. The described workflow uses ChatGPT for concept exploration, Stable Diffusion for images, and Photoshop or Illustrator for post-processing (p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 6, section 3.4.2). Assignment counts: p. 4, section 3.1; analyzed counts: p. 8, Table 1.

arms.name: Control group (traditional tools)
arms.description: No AIGC assistance. Participants researched literature and existing products on the internet, sketched, modeled and rendered designs, and used conventional software including Photoshop, Illustrator, Rhinoceros, KeyShot and Autodesk Maya (p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 6, section 3.4.3). Coded other_aid because the comparison includes internet research and conventional design aids. Assignment counts: p. 4, section 3.1; analyzed counts: p. 8, Table 1.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition are reported. Table 1 analyzes 32 students per arm, matching the assignment counts in section 3.1; no intention-to-treat designation is stated (p. 4, section 3.1; p. 8, Table 1).
participants.who: Third-year undergraduate students from Product Design and Visual Communication Design programs at a public university in Eastern China, all enrolled in a Design Innovation course. The study was conducted during the Spring semester of 2024 (March to June); recruitment dates are not separately stated. Participants had foundational design, sketching and modeling coursework but no prior formal training using AIGC tools for design (p. 4, section 3.1).
participants.quote: The study included a total of 64 participants, with 32 in the experimental group and 32 in the control group.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 3.1 Participants (sample and randomized arm counts); p. 7, section 3.7 Quantitative analysis results (quoted analyzed sample); p. 8, Table 1 (32 analyzed per arm, total 64).

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion; specific model versions are not stated (p. 4, section 3.2.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Participants used multiple rounds of ChatGPT dialogue for concept ideation, functions, interaction methods, technological approaches, examples and optimization suggestions, then generated design images with Stable Diffusion and adjusted generation parameters. Photoshop or Illustrator supported post-processing. Midjourney is listed among the available tools, and an interview account also reports using it to turn concepts into visual effects (p. 11, Table 3, Design idea development). The role code records image generation; open-chat ideation and refinement were also part of the intervention (p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 6, section 3.4.2).

task.description: Design an intelligent walking cane for elderly people or people with mobility impairments, incorporating functionality, intelligent features, ergonomic considerations, esthetic appeal, technological innovation, and the paper's stated requirement of "sustainable durability". Required deliverables were design sketches, three-dimensional models and rendered images (p. 6, section 3.4.1).
task.duration: 3 h for the design task (p. 6, section 3.4.1).

outcomes.name: Creative performance (Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale composite)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three design-field experts independently scored submitted creative works with the 30-item Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale (CSDS). Items use ratings from 1 to 5; the paper describes weighted-average dimension scores and a possible creative-performance score of 150, with higher scores indicating better performance. The dimensions are Relevance and Effectiveness, Novelty, Elegance, and Genesis (pp. 5-6, section 3.3.1). Only aggregate creative-performance results are reported by arm; no separate dimension estimates are given (pp. 8-9, Tables 1-2). The analysis uses one creative-performance score per participant (p. 8, Table 1 and section 3.7; p. 9, Figure 4). Aggregation across raters and rater blinding are not stated; the blinded interviewer described on p. 10 is not identified as a creative-output rater. Creative performance is RQ1, but neither a preregistered nor an explicitly designated primary outcome is reported (p. 2, research questions; pp. 4-7, methods). Figures 4-5 display the same scores and their relationships with EEG measures, rather than additional creative-output outcomes (pp. 9-10).

contrasts.reported: Experimental group: Mean = 115.13, Std. Deviation = 6.440, N = 32; Control group: Mean = 110.69, Std. Deviation = 9.372, N = 32 (Table 1). Mean difference = 4.438; 95% confidence interval of difference: Lower = 0.419, Upper = 8.456; Sig. (2-tailed) = 0.031 (Table 2). Prose reports t(62) = 2.208, p = 0.031, Cohen's d = 0.55. The interval is for the raw mean difference, not d. Table 2 prints 2.208 under df and 62 under t; the t and df labels used here follow the explicit prose. No effect size or standard error was calculated.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 1 (means, SDs and analyzed counts) and section 3.7 (t and p); p. 9, Table 2 (raw mean difference, confidence interval, p, and conflicting t/df headings); p. 11, section 4.1 (t, p and Cohen's d). Active comparator: p. 6, section 3.4.3.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria in the saved journal article. Section 3.1 explicitly states random assignment of students to AIGC versus traditional-tool conditions (p. 4); the controlled Design Innovation Laboratory setting supports lab_rct (p. 4, section 3.2.2). Section 3.2.1 on the same page calls the study quasi-experimental, and the allocation-sequence method is not described. Criterion 1 follows the explicit participant-allocation statement; author clarification of this inconsistency remains relevant to that criterion. The study analyzed 64 people, 32 per arm (p. 7, section 3.7; p. 8, Table 1). Three design experts independently scored participants’ submitted creative works using CSDS (pp. 5-6, sections 3.2.3 and 3.3.1). AI assisted production of the scored designs (p. 6, section 3.4.2), while the no-AIGC control used internet research and conventional design aids, supporting ai_vs_active (p. 6, section 3.4.3). The unavailable supplement and unreported rater aggregation/blinding do not prevent assessment of the three criteria from the main article.

one_line_finding: Among 64 analyzed design students, AIGC-assisted designs received higher expert-rated CSDS scores than traditional-tool designs (M = 115.13 versus 110.69; p = 0.031; Cohen's d = 0.55; p. 8, Table 1 and section 3.7; p. 11, section 4.1).
open_questions: The allocation-sequence method is not described, and section 3.1's explicit random-assignment statement conflicts with section 3.2.1's quasi-experimental label (p. 4). The reconciled design follows the explicit assignment statement.

The linked supplement is absent from the saved PDF, and its contents or any additional outcome statistics are not specified. Requests to both the stated Frontiers URL and the DOI URL were blocked by network permissions during reconciliation and finalization (p. 14, Supplementary material).
How the three experts' independent ratings were aggregated into each participant's score, and whether those experts were blinded to condition, are not stated (pp. 5-6, section 3.3.1).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09. Both raw forms were present and parsed. Read the complete markdown in successive chunks through its final references, and extracted and read all 15 PDF pages; the saved PDF contains no appended supplement. Checked numerical results against the PDF text and used PyMuPDF find_tables() on Tables 1-3. All creative-performance numbers are transcribed as printed; no effect size, standard error or other missing statistic was computed. Table 2's df and t headings conflict with the explicit prose on pp. 8 and 11; the form preserves the printed values and uses the prose to identify t and df. Only the aggregate CSDS outcome supplies a separately reported creative-output comparison. Its component dimensions have no separately reported estimates. EEG concentration and relaxation, their correlations with CSDS, and qualitative interview experiences do not add creative-output outcomes for the atlas questions. There is no reported comparison of similarity across different people's designs and no separate creative output produced after AI removal. Expert scoring after the task does not make these AI-assisted designs an after_ai outcome. The control's internet research supports other_aid and ai_vs_active coding (p. 6, section 3.4.3). No preregistration or explicit primary-outcome designation is reported. The data statement refers generally to the article/Supplementary material and correspondence, without a separate data repository or code URL (p. 14). Three substantive field differences are recorded: study dates (A omits dates; B calls them recruitment dates), evidence of Midjourney use (B adds an interview account), and durability versus sustainability in the task description. The screeners otherwise agree on design and assignment, arms and people counts, outcome inventory and coding, reported statistics, supplement status, sample-overlap reporting, company involvement, eligibility and finding. Equivalent wording, added supporting locators, reordered statistics flags and empty synthesis representations are not counted as disagreements. All inter-screener differences are settled from the PDF; the remaining shared reporting gaps are retained in open_questions and are not counted as unresolved inter-screener differences. Reconciliation quotes reproduce PDF text with whitespace normalized. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after reading the complete markdown in successive chunks (lines 1-634), extracting and reading all 15 PDF pages, and independently checking Tables 1-3 with PyMuPDF find_tables(). The assignment, people, and outcome challenge files each contain an empty problems array; therefore challenge_resolution is empty and n_corrected, n_rejected, and n_open are all zero. These counts concern challenge problems, not the reporting gaps in final.open_items. The current spec was checked: source.supplement is populated, this is an original experiment rather than a reanalysis, and randomized and analyzed counts remain distinguished. No recorded creative-performance statistic required correction and no missing effect size or standard error was computed. All open_questions are assessed in final.open_items; reconciliation contains no unresolved differences and is preserved unchanged.

open_items.item: The allocation-sequence method is unreported, and the explicit participant random-assignment statement conflicts with the quasi-experimental label (p. 4, sections 3.1 and 3.2.1). This bears on criterion 1: authors could describe how the assignment sequence was generated and implemented and explain the label. Current eligibility follows the explicit random-assignment statement.

The linked supplement and any additional outcome statistics remain unverified; the saved PDF has no appended or embedded supplement, and both named URL requests failed (p. 14, Supplementary material). Access to the supplement would settle its contents and whether it supplies additional outcomes or precision statistics. It is not needed to establish eligibility because the main article reports assignment, analyzed people counts, and expert scoring of produced designs.

Aggregation of the three experts’ ratings into participant scores and blinding of the output raters are not stated (pp. 5-6, sections 3.2.3 and 3.3.1); the blinded interviewer is a different role (p. 10, section 3.8). Authors could provide the scoring and blinding protocol. These gaps concern measurement and risk of bias, not whether creativity was scored on the produced output, so they do not change criterion 3.
